The Empirical Outer Product of the Scores

Source: R/expected_derivatives.R
expected_by_opg.Rd

Returns the score identity of expected_derivative_methods evaluated at each observation, with no expectation. At order 2 this is \(-\ell^{(i)}\ell^{(j)}\), the per-observation outer product of the score (the BHHH estimator of the information); at orders 3 and 4 it is the sum of products \(-\sum_{\pi,\,|\pi| \ge 2} \prod_{B \in \pi} \ell_B\). Unlike every other route it takes no expectation: it integrates nothing and sums nothing over the support, so it costs the derivatives of orders 1 to order - 1 at the observations.

Usage

expected_by_opg(distrib, y, theta, order = 2L)

Arguments

distrib

An object inheriting from class "distrib".

y

A numeric vector of observations.

theta

A named list of parameters.

order

The derivative order, 2 to 4. The default is 2.

Value

A named list of expected derivative component vectors, named as observed_deriv() names that order; each has the length of y.

Details

This route differs from the identity from which it comes. The second Bartlett identity states that \(\mathbb{E}[\ell^{(ij)}] = -\mathbb{E}[\ell^{(i)}\ell^{(j)}]\), and expected_by_bartlett() evaluates the right-hand side as written, which for a discrete family is a sum over the whole support and for a continuous one a quadrature. This function drops the expectation and reads the integrand at the observation in hand. The two agree in expectation and differ in cost: for a discrete family the identity evaluates the derivative kernel over the whole support for every observation, whereas this route evaluates it once per observation.

The estimate has more variance than the exact expectation and remains consistent: each term is an unbiased estimate of the corresponding component of the expected derivative at that observation, so the sum over observations estimates it consistently. Component by component at order 2 it is a rank-one matrix and correlates poorly with the exact expectation; summed over the observations it approximates the exact information, and a fit driven by it reaches the same maximum. At orders 3 and 4 the terms are products of up to four derivatives, and the variance is larger still.

It is the right default for a scoring step because it is a sum of outer products and is therefore positive semidefinite by construction, whereas the observed Hessian need not be positive semidefinite away from the optimum, and because the fixed point is unchanged, since the score is exact and any positive definite matrix takes a scoring iteration to the same stationary point. The route is not suited to a reported standard error, which is read off the observed information instead; see fit_distrib() and its vcov() method.

See also

expected_by_bartlett() for the identity that this function estimates, expected_derivative_methods() for the catalog of routes, and expected_hessian_exact() for the predicate that tests whether a family needs any of them.
